sections.body: This field covers ten creative disciplines where artificial intelligence is now part of making work, from images and video to music, voice, movement, text, theater, photography, interactive pieces, and questions of ownership. The site tracks 1000 live image generation models, 1000 video models, and 2000 audio models, along with 732 AI tools that artists and studios use in production. In visual arts, models turn text prompts into illustrations, while cinematography tools generate short clips and synthetic shots. Vocal synthesis produces sung or spoken performances, and music composition systems create stems, arrangements, and full tracks. Choreography tools map motion from video or sensor data, and literary systems draft narrative text. Theater and virtual set design use generated backdrops and environments, photography tools push toward hyper-real images, and interactive art responds to viewers through generated content. Rights and provenance work tracks who owns these outputs and how they were made.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work is uneven across disciplines. Image generation is widely used and mature enough for commercial illustration, but hands, text in images, and consistent characters still fail often. Video synthesis produces short, convincing clips, yet long-form continuity and physical accuracy remain unsolved. Audio models can clone voices and generate music, but emotional control and legal clarity are limited, and 18 of the 92 active intellectual property lawsuits on this site involve AI music services. Choreography and motion mapping work for simple loops but struggle with complex partnering and weight. Literary tools produce fluent drafts but not reliable plot logic over long works. Theater and virtual set design are usable for previsualization, not yet for fully autonomous live performance. Photography and hyper-realism can fool casual viewers, while detection and provenance tools lag behind. Interactive and experiential art is experimental, often built for single installations rather than repeatable systems. The honest limit is that these tools assist and remix, they do not yet understand meaning, style, or intent.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader looking at how images are made would start with Visual Arts and Generative Illustration, then move to Photography and Hyper-Realism for the boundary between generated and captured work. Cinematography and Video Synthesis covers moving images, while Theater and Virtual Set Design shows how those same tools build environments for stage work. Vocal Synthesis and Operatic Performance pairs with Music Composition and Audio Engineering, since voice and instrumental generation share models and legal questions. Choreography and Motion Mapping connects movement to the same motion data used in video and interactive pieces. Literary Arts and Narrative Design covers text, and Interactive and Experiential Art shows how all of these outputs can be combined in responsive installations. Rights and Provenance in AI Art is the page to read last, because it explains the ownership and attribution problems raised by every other page, including the 92 active intellectual property lawsuits tracked on this site.
